paras.text: Contractors, Liens and Assignment of Benefits in Claims: Audio Lecture

Welcome to the chapter on contractors, liens, and assignment of benefits. Three bodies of Michigan law collide inside a single restoration job: the Construction Lien Act, which governs how a contractor gets paid by the homeowner; the Insurance Code, which governs the homeowner's claim against the carrier; and old-fashioned assignment law, which governs whether the contractor can step into the homeowner's shoes and deal with the carrier directly. Get any one of these wrong and the contractor can do excellent work and collect nothing for it.

Let's start with the case that anchors this whole chapter. Epps versus four Quarters Restoration, four ninety eight Michigan five eighteen, decided in twenty fifteen. A home in Detroit floods in two thousand six. The homeowners, Danny and Joyce Epps, are referred to a man named Troy Willis and his companies, four Quarters Restoration and Emergency Insurance Services. Willis is not a licensed residential builder when he does the work. His builder's license had been revoked on January thirty first of two thousand six, and he did not tell the Epps that. The Epps sign a repair agreement assigning the insurance proceeds to Willis's company. Willis went on to receive and endorse Auto Owners checks totaling one hundred twenty eight thousand and forty seven dollars, signing the Epps' names himself. If that sounds like a modern assignment of benefits arrangement, that's because it basically is one.

The Michigan Supreme Court had to answer a basic-sounding question: is a contract with an unlicensed builder void, meaning it never legally existed, or voidable, meaning it's valid unless and until someone chooses to void it? If void, neither side has any rights under it. The Court held that contracts between an innocent homeowner and an unlicensed residential builder are voidable, not void, correcting sloppier language in older opinions.

Now here's the nuance that most summaries of this case get wrong, and it's worth slowing down for. The word "innocent" in that holding is not decorative. The Michigan Supreme Court expressly limited its ruling to a homeowner who did not know the contractor was unlicensed. In the Epps' own case, there was no indication in the record that they knew Willis was unlicensed, so the Court said its analysis was limited to that fact pattern. The Court did not decide what happens if a homeowner knowingly hires an unlicensed contractor. So if you ever hear someone say "Epps means the voidable rule applies no matter what the homeowner knew," that is an overstatement of the actual holding.

There's a second piece of Epps that's completely separate from the void-versus-voidable question, and it genuinely does not care what the homeowner knew. The statute at issue, M C L three thirty nine point twenty four twelve, subsection one, says an unlicensed contractor cannot bring or maintain a lawsuit to collect compensation without alleging and proving it was licensed during performance. No knowledge exception anywhere in the text. The Michigan Supreme Court described this rule using a phrase borrowed from an earlier Court of Appeals case, Parker versus McQuade Plumbing and Heating: the statute operates as "a shield, not a sword." It removes the unlicensed contractor's power to sue. It does not remove the contractor's power to defend itself if the homeowner sues first, and it does not hand the homeowner an independent right to sue the unlicensed contractor to get money back. The Court specifically declined to read that private right of action into the statute. So remember the two-part structure: the suit-bar under subsection one is absolute and knowledge-independent; the void-versus-voidable classification of the contract itself was decided only for the innocent-homeowner scenario.

That same statute, subsection three, also says an unlicensed contractor cannot impose a construction lien on the property, and subsection four lets a prosecutor or the attorney general sue for a civil fine of not less than five thousand and not more than twenty five thousand dollars. Licensing isn't a technicality; it's the foundation everything else here sits on.

Now let's move to the Construction Lien Act rules for residential work, because a restoration job is almost always residential. M C L five seventy point eleven fourteen says a contractor has no right to a construction lien on a homeowner's property unless the improvement was done under a written contract, with any amendments also in writing, and that contract states, in type no smaller than the body of the contract, that the work requires a license and, if it does, that the contractor is licensed and the actual license number. There is no dollar floor. Miss the license number and the lien is gone, even if the contractor is genuinely licensed.

Then there are three clocks you need cold. Twenty days: a subcontractor or supplier has to serve a Notice of Furnishing within twenty days after furnishing the first labor or material, under M C L five seventy point eleven zero nine. But, a favorite trap, a contractor in direct contract with the homeowner does not have to serve this notice at all. The twenty-day clock is for subs and suppliers, not the general contractor dealing straight with the owner. Ninety days: under M C L five seventy point eleven eleven, the right to a construction lien ceases to exist unless a claim of lien is recorded with the register of deeds within ninety days after the lien claimant's last furnishing of labor or material. That's a hard, absolute deadline. One year: under M C L five seventy point eleven seventeen, once you've recorded that claim of lien, you have to file suit to foreclose it within one year of the recording date, or the lien expires. One more clock to keep separate: a laborer, as opposed to a subcontractor or supplier, gets thirty days after wages were due but unpaid, under subsection two of eleven zero nine. Layered on top is M C L five seventy point eleven ten, the sworn statement rule: a contractor has to give the owner a sworn statement listing every sub, supplier, and unpaid laborer whenever payment is due, requested, or demanded. Lie on it with intent to defraud, and that's a crime.

Now let's turn to the assignment of benefits question, because this is where most of the confusion in a restoration practice actually lives. Michigan has never passed a statute specifically regulating assignment of benefits for property insurance. There is no A O B statute here at all. The entire doctrine is common law, and it goes all the way back to eighteen eighty. The case is Roger Williams Insurance Company versus Carrington, forty three Michigan two fifty two. A livery stable's fire insurance policy covered property that burned down. After the fire, the insured assigned the policy to secure a debt, without asking the insurance company's permission. The company said the policy's anti-assignment clause voided the whole thing. The Michigan Supreme Court disagreed, and the language it used is still quoted by Michigan courts today: the assignment, having been made after the loss, did not require the company's consent, and a policy provision forfeiting coverage for an unconsented assignment is invalid as applied to the transfer of an already-accrued claim. The Court called it "the absolute right of every person" to assign such a claim, and said preventing that right would be against public policy.

That rule got a modern restatement in twenty eighteen, in Jawad A. Shah, M.D., P C, versus State Farm, three twenty four Michigan Appeals one eighty two. This is a no-fault case, not a property case. Healthcare providers had taken an assignment of a patient's no-fault benefits after treating him, but the Court of Appeals leaned directly on Roger Williams to reach the same result. State Farm's policy said no assignment of benefits was binding without its approval. The Court held that clause unenforceable, because the assignment here was of an accrued claim, made after the loss, for services already provided. The Court was careful to say this isn't about the clause being "unreasonable." Michigan generally enforces clear contract language as written under Rory versus Continental. This is narrower: enforcing an anti-assignment clause against a genuinely post-loss transfer of an accrued claim violates the same public policy identified in eighteen eighty. For your restoration practice: if a homeowner signs an assignment of benefits for work already done, an anti-assignment clause in her policy cannot block it. But that protection is narrow. It does not extend to a pre-loss transfer of the policy itself, and it says nothing about whether the contractor can act as the adjuster once it has the assignment. That's a separate question, and the answer to it is no.

Here's where a lot of restoration companies get themselves in real trouble. An assignment of benefits gives a contractor standing to sue the carrier as an assignee, stepping into the homeowner's contractual shoes for the assigned, accrued claim. It does not create any new rights the homeowner didn't already have, and it does not license the contractor to negotiate or adjust the claim. M C L five hundred point twelve twenty two says a person cannot adjust loss or damage under a policy, or hold themselves out as an adjuster, without a license, with exactly five exemptions: Michigan attorneys, marine average adjusters, an insurer's own employees, a licensed producer with granted claim authority, and a narrow supervised data-entry role. A restoration contractor is not on that list, assignment or not.

This is exactly the mistake that got a real Michigan adjuster in real trouble. DIFS case number twenty five, dash, one eight three five zero, involves an adjuster named Aleksandr Guldshtadt. He was summarily suspended in November of twenty twenty five, and the final decision issued April first of twenty twenty six revoked his license outright and ordered him to pay a fifty thousand dollar civil fine. He held a financial interest in a fire repair contractor, used adjusting contracts DIFS had never approved, let unlicensed people sign consumers up, and diverted claim money to a contracting business he had an interest in. DIFS charged that under M C L five hundred point twelve twenty six, and reached his license through twelve twenty four, subsection three, plus twelve forty two, subsection two. Separately, subsection four of twelve twenty four is the flat rule that a person connected with a fire repair contractor cannot be issued an adjuster license at all. A restoration company with an assignment of benefits that negotiates a disputed scope for a percentage fee is walking that exact same line.

Now, the twelve percent penalty interest question. M C L five hundred point two thousand six, subsection four, says an insurer owes twelve percent simple interest on a late-paid claim, belonging to "the insured or a person directly entitled to benefits." No published Michigan property-insurance case has decided whether a contractor holding an assignment of benefits counts as "a person directly entitled to benefits" in its own right. So don't promise that twelve percent as an automatic entitlement for the contractor. The honest framing: the contractor pursues it derivatively, standing in the homeowner's shoes, because the homeowner's own right survives the assignment. That's meaningfully different from claiming the contractor owns the twelve percent outright.

Next, the Michigan Consumer Protection Act, because people reach for it constantly when frustrated with a carrier, and it almost never works. The general exemption is M C L four forty five point nine zero four, subsection one, letter A: the act doesn't apply to conduct specifically authorized under laws administered by a regulatory board. The case usually cited here is Smith versus Globe Life Insurance Company, four sixty Michigan four forty six, from nineteen ninety nine, but that case is usually oversimplified. In nineteen ninety nine, the version of the statute then in force had a carve-out permitting certain private actions for chapter twenty insurance-code conduct, and that's specifically why the plaintiff's M C P A claim survived in Smith. The legislature closed that carve-out afterward. The current version, M C L four forty five point nine zero four, subsection three, says the act does not apply to, or create a cause of action for, unfair or deceptive practices made unlawful by chapter twenty of the insurance code, for conduct on or after March twenty eighth, two thousand one. So today, current law bars an M C P A claim against an insurer's claims-handling conduct. Smith isn't wrong, it's describing a rule since closed.

If you end up in court over a small unpaid balance, know the venue rules. M C L six hundred point eighty four zero one sets Michigan's small claims jurisdictional limit at seven thousand dollars, effective January first, two thousand twenty four, up from five thousand dollars back in twenty twelve. M C L six hundred point eighty four zero eight says attorneys cannot participate except on their own behalf, so no lawyers on either side, unless a party removes the case to the general civil division before trial.

Last piece: rescission rights on work authorizations signed during a loss. Two different statutes, two different windows, easy to mix up. The Home Improvement Finance Act, or HIFA, applies only when the homeowner is financing the job on installment credit through the contractor, cash price over three hundred dollars. Its rescission window, under M C L four forty five point twelve zero two, is short: until five p.m. on the business day following the date of the contract, roughly one business day. The Home Solicitation Sales Act, or HSSA, applies when the contractor solicited the sale at the homeowner's residence, think a door-knocking storm-damage salesperson. Its window, under M C L four forty five point one one two, is three business days, running to midnight. A homeowner who calls a contractor herself after a pipe bursts hasn't been "solicited," so HSSA doesn't automatically apply.

HSSA has an emergency exception mitigation companies rely on constantly, with three conditions that must all be met. The seller has to, in good faith, substantially begin performance before any cancellation notice. For goods, they have to be un-returnable in substantially as-good condition. And critically, the homeowner has to give a separate, dated, signed personal statement, written in her own handwriting, describing the emergency and expressly waiving the three-day right. A typed waiver clause at the bottom of the standard work order does not satisfy this. It has to be a separate page, written by hand, by the homeowner. Skip that step and the homeowner keeps a live cancellation right for three business days, even while the drying equipment is already running in her basement.

Let's recap the numbers. Ninety days to record a construction lien after last furnishing labor or material. One year to foreclose it after recording. Twenty days for a subcontractor's notice of furnishing, zero days for a contractor in direct contract with the owner. Voidable, not void, for an unlicensed contractor's contract with an innocent homeowner, but "innocent" is doing real legal work, so don't extend it further than the Court did. Post-loss assignment of an accrued claim survives an anti-assignment clause, back to eighteen eighty, but that protection stops at pre-loss transfers. Twelve percent interest belongs to the insured, pursued by the contractor only derivatively. No Michigan Consumer Protection Act claim for chapter twenty insurance conduct after March of two thousand one. Seven thousand dollars is today's small claims ceiling, no lawyers allowed there. One business day to rescind under HIFA, three business days under HSSA, and a handwritten waiver, not a typed one, to cut that HSSA window short in a genuine emergency. Lock these numbers in, and you'll never confuse getting paid for the work with getting to adjust the claim. Two different licenses, two different bodies of law, and confusing them is exactly how a good contractor ends up in front of DIFS.
